source: Zeller (2009) Why Programs Fail, 2nd ed. (Scientific Debugging chapter)
finding: Zeller states debugging as the scientific method. Keep a log of hypothesis, prediction, experiment, observation, conclusion. A refuted hypothesis is still progress; a confirmed one narrows the cause. The AutoSD paper (opened) confirms this five-part list.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Five log items: hypothesis, prediction, experiment, observation, conclusion (confirmed via the AutoSD paper's description).
limits: A prescriptive method from a textbook, not an experiment. No test that following it makes people faster. Book itself not opened this session.
agent_relevance: The model for a predict-then-observe check: write the expected result before running, compare after. Code can enforce the order.

source: Siegmund et al. as cited by Kang et al. (2023): developers follow hypothesis then verification without training
finding: A survey study reported that developers, even with no formal debugging training, roughly follow hypothesis formulation then verification. Seen only as a citation inside the AutoSD paper.
numbers: No numbers seen. Secondary citation only.
limits: Contrasts with Li and Coblenz 2026 (see SUBFIELDS.md): observed professionals rarely state formal testable hypotheses. Self-report vs observation gap.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the textbook method is natural for the model. It has to be imposed by the scaffold.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (2-4-6)
finding: People testing a rule mostly propose instances that fit their hypothesis and rarely try to break it. This is the root of weak experiments in debugging: tests that can only confirm.
numbers: From memory, not verified: 29 participants; about 6 announced the right rule at the first attempt; most announced one or more wrong rules first.
limits: Not opened. Numbers from memory, so treat as approximate. Later work (Klayman and Ha 1987) shows positive tests are often a sound heuristic when the true rule is narrow.
agent_relevance: Guardrail G3 matches this: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to. A prediction that could only confirm is weak.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Positive test strategy (test cases the hypothesis says will happen) is not irrational; it is informative when the hypothesis is narrower than the truth. It fails when the hypothesis is too broad, which is the usual case for a wrong bug guess.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened. Competing explanation to a simple 'confirmation bias' story.
agent_relevance: Prediction should be chosen so that the two hypotheses disagree about it, not merely so that the favourite is supported.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning (SDDS)
finding: Scientific reasoning is search in two linked spaces: a hypothesis space and an experiment space. Participants programming a toy robot (BigTrak) split into theorists, who favour hypotheses, and experimenters, who favour experiments. Each loop is: form hypothesis, run experiment, evaluate evidence.
numbers: From memory, not verified: about 20 adult participants on the BigTrak repeat-key task. Exact group counts not checked.
limits: Full text not reachable this session (publisher pages returned 403, CMU copy 404). Treat details as unverified.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal skeleton for our S3/S4 loop: pick hypothesis, pick a discriminating experiment, evaluate. The program, not the model, should own the loop.

source: Gould (1975) Some psychological evidence on how people debug computer programs
finding: Early lab study: programmers debugging Fortran bugs. Bugs that need a wrong value traced back (assignment, data) took far longer than wrong-statement bugs. Founding evidence that debugging is hypothesis testing about code state.
numbers: Not verified. About 14 programmers and 12 bugs is my recollection only.
limits: Not opened; numbers uncertain.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Experts differ from novices by keeping a system-level view and by changing strategy when a line of attack fails; novices go depth-first and stay stuck. Experts' hypotheses are revised, novices' persist.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened; small-sample think-aloud study.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: change approach on a failure signal, not on a clock.

source: Gugerty and Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers
finding: Experts found bugs faster and more often. Novices introduced new bugs when fixing. Experts generated better hypotheses from reading code (comprehension), not from trial and error. Covered by the sibling subfield 'Gugerty and Olson findings'.
numbers: Not verified; do not quote numbers.
limits: Not opened. Language was LOGO and Pascal; small groups.
agent_relevance: Note only; sibling subfield owns it.

source: Katz and Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies
finding: Strategies for locating a bug differ with who wrote the code: for your own code people reason from the symptom backward; for someone else's they comprehend forward. Bug location and bug repair are separate skills.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened; Lisp, student participants.
agent_relevance: Supports separating 'locate' from 'repair' states.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Human study of ranked fault localisation tools. Programmers did not follow the ranked list in order, and the tool helped on an easy bug but not on a harder one; checking a candidate line did not mean they saw the bug.
numbers: Not verified. I recall 34 participants and 2 bugs; unchecked.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a recollection.
agent_relevance: Shows that handing a location is not enough; the hypothesis must be tested. Consistent with Alaboudi and LaToza 2020 in SUBFIELDS.md.

source: Zeller and Hildebrandt (2002) Simplifying and isolating failure-inducing input (delta debugging)
finding: Delta debugging automates the experiment step: run the program on reduced inputs, observe pass or fail, shrink to a minimal failing case. It is a mechanical hypothesis tester with no model of the cause.
numbers: Not verified; I recall reductions of whole failing inputs to a few characters.
limits: Not opened. Needs a clear pass/fail test and a deterministic run.
agent_relevance: A code-run operator we could give the agent: minimise the failing case before reasoning about it.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented: asking and answering why and why not questions about program behavior (ICSE)
finding: Whyline for Java lets programmers ask why did / why didn't about output, and answers from a recorded trace. In the lab study, users of the Whyline were about twice as fast on debugging tasks as users of standard tools.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 20 participants, two bugs in a larger Java program.
limits: Not opened; the PDF URLs tried returned 404. Study used mostly novice-to-intermediate Java programmers.
agent_relevance: The question form 'why did X not happen' is itself a prediction that failed. Our O5 backwards-from-failure operator is this.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: a debugging interface for asking questions about program behavior (CHI)
finding: Debugging is an inquisitive loop: hypothesise, observe, restructure, explore, diagnose, repair. Current tools support observation but not hypothesising. In earlier Alice studies, half of all errors came from false assumptions in programmers' own hypotheses.
numbers: 50% of all errors were due to false assumptions in hypotheses formed while debugging. 68% of questions were why didn't, 32% why did. 85% concerned a single object.
quote: If programmers have a weak hypothesis about the cause of a failure, any implicit assumptions about what
limits: Alice, a teaching language; Pac-Man task; participants were HCI masters students.
agent_relevance: Half of new errors in debugging come from a wrong belief, not a wrong edit. Check beliefs by observation before editing.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: user study (With 5 vs Without 4 participants, 90 minutes)
finding: Alice programmers with the Whyline finished more tasks in 90 minutes and debugged much faster than without it. Programmers without it hypothesised by inspecting and rewriting code; with it, by asking questions and reading the answer.
numbers: Tasks completed: M=3.20 (SD .457) with vs M=2.25 (SD .500) without, t(7)=3.0, p<.02, a 40% increase. Debugging time over six matched scenarios: F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02, average factor 7.8 faster. Whyline useful for 19 of 24 questions; 0 of 3 for the first user, 5 of 5 for the fifth.
limits: Tiny sample (9 people in two between-group studies); a design iteration, so the tool changed between users. Not a randomised trial.
agent_relevance: Making the hypothesis checkable by cheap observation changes speed by large factors. Our agent should run a probe, not reason about it.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: AutoSD makes a chatbot (ChatGPT) follow Zeller's loop: write a hypothesis plus a debugger command (pdb/jdb) that tests it, run the command for real, feed back the output, then conclude. A <DONE> token marks enough evidence; then the patch is written. Repair rate stays level with a plain LLM while giving a readable trace.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2 correct fixes: Recoder 24, InCoder 41, LLM-Base 87, AutoSD 76. Defects4J v2.0: 11, 28, 110, 113. ARHE (self-built Almost-Right HumanEval): plausible LLM-Base 179 vs AutoSD 189; correct 177 vs 187. 10 patches per bug.
quote: prompts large language models to automatically generate hypotheses, uses debuggers to actively interact with buggy code
limits: Not clearly better than the plain LLM on Defects4J v1.2 (76 vs 87). ChatGPT-era model, possible data leakage on Defects4J (the authors built ARHE to avoid it). Main aim is explanation, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Shows the hypothesis/run/observe loop costs little accuracy and gives a trace. It does not prove an accuracy gain.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD: debugger ablation and <DONE> confidence
finding: Real execution output is what makes the loop work. When the model imagined debugger output instead of getting real output, the confidence signal flipped and the plausible-patch rate fell. Strong direct support for observing, not predicting.
numbers: Real execution: <DONE>-predicted fixes were 12.4 percentage points more likely to be plausible. Hallucinated debugger: 11 points less likely. Individual runs plausible: 73% with real debugger vs 63% without. Among plausible patches, 89% correct with <DONE> vs 82% without. Defects4J check used 100 sampled patches per group.
limits: ARHE and Defects4J only; a single model family (ChatGPT) for the ablation.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: revise from real output. A written prediction is only useful if the next step gets a real observation to compare it with.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD: developer study of patch review with and without explanations
finding: 20 people reviewed AI patches with or without the scientific-debugging trace. Same time, higher accuracy on 5 of 6 real bugs. Two cases got worse: a trace was accepted without scrutiny, or made people over-cautious.
numbers: N=20 (8 undergrads, 6 grad students, 6 professionals, 3-10 years). 6 problems each in 30-40 min; 12 problems total (6 ARHE, 6 BugsInPy). Accuracy higher with explanation in 7 of 12 cases (5 from BugsInPy), lower in 2 (ARHE105, BIP003). Time not significantly different in any case. Explanation rated helpful in 8 of 12. 70% said explanations are important; 55% satisfied with the scientific-debugging format.
limits: Small N, no inferential tests on accuracy given. Risk: a convincing trace can mislead (ARHE105).
agent_relevance: A trace that looks scientific can raise trust without raising correctness. The check must be a run, not a persuasive story (G5).

source: Chen, Wang, Nye, Zhou (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug (rubber duck)
finding: Few-shot prompt: run the code, then have the model explain the code line by line (rubber duck) and read execution results, then fix. Gains are largest with unit-test execution results; explanation helps most where no tests exist.
numbers: Spider (Codex) 81.3 baseline to 84.1 with explanation. MBPP: Codex 61.4 to 70.8 best, GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6. TransCoder: Codex 80.4 to 92.5 best. Sample efficiency: debugging a greedy sample matches 16 samples on Spider; from 8 samples beats baseline at 32. Usually one debugging turn is enough.
quote: explaining the code line-by-line in natural language to a rubber duck significantly boosts debugging efficiency
limits: Table cell labels are garbled in the extracted text, so best-value attributions are approximate. On Spider without tests, simple feedback alone did not help much because the model could not tell right from wrong answers.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback is the active ingredient; explanation adds a smaller gain. Do not rely on self-judgement without a run.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) LDB: a Large Language Model Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step-by-step
finding: LDB splits a failing program into basic blocks, prints the values of variables after each block, and asks the model for a verdict (correct or wrong) per block against the task. It is like setting breakpoints and checking each state against what was expected. It beats self-explanation and self-trace prompts.
numbers: HumanEval seeds: GPT-3.5 73.8 -> LDB 82.9 (+9.1), Self-Debug 81.1; GPT-4 87.2 -> 89.6, Self-Debug 88.4; Reflexion seeds 91.5 -> 95.1 (new best then), Self-Debug 92.1. Gains up to 9.8% over baseline across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. Self-Debug stalls after 2-3 rounds while LDB keeps improving across 10.
quote: LDB segments programs into basic blocks and tracks the values of intermediate variables after each block throughout runtime execution
limits: Debugging backbone GPT-3.5 in the main table. Bug-localisation correctness judged by GPT-4, not by humans.
agent_relevance: Block-level check of real values against the intended state is a direct predict-then-observe step. Self-explanation alone plateaus; real values do not.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR)
finding: At equal compute, self-repair often beats plain resampling only slightly, and sometimes not at all. The bottleneck is the model's own feedback (diagnosis). Better feedback from a stronger model or a human boosts it a lot.
numbers: Human study: 16 participants, 2 feedback strings per each of 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 repair samples per feedback. Overall repair success 33.30% with GPT-4's own feedback vs 52.60% with human feedback (1.58x). By difficulty: introductory 42.64 vs 62.21, interview 19.33 vs 45.67, competition 3.67 vs 14.67. APPS: GPT-4 self-repair beat baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 marginal.
limits: Models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama; single-turn repair tree; human feedback written by participants who spent about an hour.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis (the hypothesis) is the limiting step, matching Alaboudi and LaToza 2020. Spend effort where the hypothesis is formed, and make it testable.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Gains from self-correction in earlier papers came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop. Without the oracle (intrinsic self-correction), accuracy fell. The model cannot judge its own answer without outside evidence.
numbers: With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5. Intrinsic, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. Intrinsic, GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Reasoning tasks (math, QA), not code with tests. Does not say that execution feedback fails; it says that feedback with no outside signal fails.
agent_relevance: A prediction written by the model and then judged by the same model is not a test. The observation must come from code. (G2, G3, G5)

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: a text-based environment for interactive debugging (Microsoft)
finding: Agents given the Python debugger (pdb) to set breakpoints and print values do not reliably do better. Strong models gain on real GitHub issues; weak models are hurt. Giving the debugger only after 5 failed rewrites worked best.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite success % (rewrite / debug / debug(5), 3 runs): GPT-4o 19.1/17.2/23.6; GPT-4o-mini 4.0/3.5/6.2; o1-preview 10.7/30.2/30.8; o3-mini 8.5/22.1/19.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 37.2/48.4/52.1; Llama-3.3-70B 2.4/4.0/4.8. Aider (133 simple tasks): no clear gain, e.g. GPT-4o 76.4/69.7/72.9. Mini-nightmare (10 tricky bugs): GPT-4o 40.0/40.0/53.3; Llama-3.3-70B 0/0/0.
limits: Minimal prompts, no hypothesis scaffold; the paper tests tool access, not predict-then-observe. Mini-nightmare has only 10 tasks. Column assignment from a garbled table, so approximate. Authors say agents are still far from using the tools well.
agent_relevance: Tools alone do not give scientific debugging. Models need a loop that forces a hypothesis and a check. Introducing the probe only after an impasse (debug(5)) matches G1: doubt on a signal.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching Large Language Models to Reason about Code Execution (ICML)
finding: Fine-tune a model to write natural-language rationales that read execution traces (variable values per line) and then fix the bug. Self-trained on its own correct fixes. Trace-aware rationales help; removing the trace in training hurts.
numbers: PaLM 2-L fix rate improved by 26.1% absolute on Mbpp-R and 14.3% on HumanEvalFix+ (pass@1). Beats GPT-3.5 on all pass@k. Human rating on 104 Mbpp-R tasks: rationales better than base PaLM 2 and on par with GPT-3.5.
limits: Needs training, so not a scaffold-only result. PaLM 2-L only. Traces limited to program states and variable values.
agent_relevance: Evidence that reading real traces is the thing to scaffold, not free reasoning. We cannot train, but we can paste real traces into the slot.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: Tests whether models can predict what a program will do: coverage, program state, execution path, output. Models do worst on execution path and are often inconsistent: right output with wrong path. So their predictions about execution are not reliable evidence.
numbers: Average accuracy 44.4% on runtime behavior reasoning; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3. GPT-4-Turbo best, 19.3 points above second best (GPT-3.5 55.7%). Open-source best (CodeLlama-34B-Instruct) 51.0%. Output prediction above 50% for every model; only 8 of 15 reach 10% on execution path.
limits: Short functions from HumanEval and ClassEval; 15 models, mostly 2023-24 era.
agent_relevance: The prediction half of predict-then-observe is weak when models predict execution; the check is what makes it informative. Disagreement between predicted and observed is the signal.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: a benchmark for code reasoning, understanding and execution
finding: 800 short Python functions; the model must predict the output from the input, or an input from the output. Good HumanEval scores did not translate. Even with chain of thought, the best model gets about three-quarters to four-fifths.
numbers: GPT-4 with CoT: pass@1 75% (input prediction) and 81% (output prediction). Code Llama 34B: 50% and 46%. 20 models tested.
limits: Abstract and intro read; method details not read. Functions are 3-13 lines, far from real bugs.
agent_relevance: Calibration: even a strong model mispredicts execution of a 13-line function about one time in five. Never trust a self-made prediction in place of a run.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (ICLR)
finding: Correction guided by external tools (code interpreter, search) improves answers; correction with only the model's own critique does not. Matches Huang et al. on the point that outside evidence is what works.
numbers: Tested on ChatGPT, text-davinci-003 and LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B on QA, math program synthesis and toxicity. Only the abstract, intro and result summaries were read, not the full tables.
limits: Partly read; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: correction needs real outside output.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD: effect of model strength and failure causes
finding: The scientific-debugging loop depends on the model being strong enough to follow it. With a bigger or better model its repair count rises quickly. The common failure was choosing the wrong breakpoint, so the experiment could not see the faulty state.
numbers: Models compared: CodeGen-6B, Codex (code-davinci-002), ChatGPT. Exact per-model counts only in a figure, not read. Authors: AutoSD becomes comparable to the plain LLM as the model improves. 6 qualitative cases; liked trace BIP006 75% liked, disliked trace BIP002 16% liked.
limits: Figure values not extracted. Interface and linking to specs were named by participants as weak points.
agent_relevance: A weak model cannot run the loop; the program must choose or check the probe (a probe that cannot show the faulty state is a wasted experiment).
